thread.title: Crash Protection Kicks In For Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: David Pinsen
title: Crash Protection Kicks In For Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple fans in Toronto queue for a new iPhone (via Business Insider ).
Apple Gets Soft In early August, I presented two ways Apple ( AAPL ) longs could limit their downside risk ("Make Way For MAGA"). Since then, the stock has dropped 28.8%.
AAPL Total Return Price data by YCharts
Let's look at how those August hedges have ameliorated Apple's drop since and talk briefly about what hedged Apple longs can do now. First, though, a quick reminder about the purpose of hedging: You hedge when you are bullish about a security (otherwise you wouldn't own it) but want to limit your risk in the event you were wrong. Apple longs who hedged in August didn't expect the stock to drop significantly but wanted to protect themselves in case it did.
The August Optimal Put Hedge On Aug. 1, these were the optimal, or least expensive, puts to hedge 200 shares of AAPL against a greater-than-20% drop by mid-February (optimal hedge screen captures were via the Portfolio Armor iPhone app).
Note that the cost here was $428, or 1.06% of position value (calculated conservatively, using the ask price of the puts).
Let's look at how that hedge has reacted to the 28.8% drop.
How The Optimal Put Hedge Has Reacted Here's an updated quote on those puts as of Thursday's close:
Screen capture via the CBOE.
How That Hedge Ameliorated Apple's Drop Apple closed at $201.50 on Aug. 1. A shareholder who owned 200 shares of it and hedged with the puts above then had $40,300 in AAPL shares plus $428 in puts, so the net position value was $40,300 + $428 = $40,728.
The stock closed at $142.19 on Thursday, Jan. 3, down 28.8% from its close on Aug. 1. The investors' shares were worth $28,433 on Thursday, and the put options were worth $4,830, using the midpoint of the spread. So, the net position value as of Thursday's close was $28,433 + $4,830 = $33,263. $33,263 represents a 18.3% drop from $40,728.
The August Optimal Collar Hedge On Aug. 1, this was the optimal collar to protect against a >20% drop in 200 shares of AAPL by mid-February, while not capping your possible upside at less than 16% by then.
In this case, the net cost of the hedge was negative, meaning you would have collected an $42 net credit, assuming, conservatively, that you bought the puts and sold the calls at the worst ends of their respective spreads.
How That Optimal Collar Hedge Has Reacted Here's an update quote on the put leg of the collar, which, in this case, is at the same strike as the previous hedge:
Screen capture via the CBOE.
And here's an updated quote on the call leg:
Screen capture via the CBOE.
How That Hedge Ameliorated Apple's Drop Recall that Apple closed at $201.50 on Aug. 1. A shareholder who owned 200 shares of it and hedged with the collar above then had $40,300 in AAPL shares plus $428 in puts, and if the investor wanted to buy to close the short call position, it would have cost him $470. So, his net position value on Aug. 1. was ($40,300 + $428) - $470 = $40,258.
On Thursday, the shares were worth $28,433 , the put options were worth $4,830, and it would have cost $6 to buy to close his calls, using the midpoint of the spread in both cases. So ($28,433 + $4,830) - $6 = $33,257. $33,257 represents a 17.4% drop from $40,258.
A Bit More Protection Than Promised In Both Cases AAPL dropped by 28.8% from Aug. 1 to Jan. 3. Both hedges were designed to protect against a >20% drop, and they limited drawdowns to 18.3% and 17.4%, respectively, thanks in part to the time value of the put options.
What Now? Seeking Alpha's editors have put together a convenient roundup of bullish and bearish reactions to Apple's revenue warning that led to Thursday's ~10% drop. If you're long Apple and hedged, I would take the time to review both of those roundups. Another source of guidance you might consider is the social data mining firm LikeFolio. I wrote about how their analysis of purchase intent helped them anticipate a strong quarter from Tesla's ( TSLA ) last year (" Tesla: Who Got It Right "). Similarly, the analysis of Apple's purchase intent after its keynote in September signaled weakness in advance of this week's revenue warning.
The nice thing about being hedged, though, is that you don't have to worry so much about how much further the shares might drop (you're not going to be down more than 20% with these hedges). If you're bearish on Apple now, you can exit for a smaller loss. If you're bullish and think this is a bottom, you can sell your appreciated puts and buy more shares. In any case, you have breathing space to let the dust settle and decide on your best course of action without the anxiety of an unhedged investor.
